items.name: Ferrari
clues: It sells something very few people need and a lot of people want, and it makes sure there are never quite enough to go round.
Very rich people, many of whom have to show they are loyal customers before they are allowed to buy the newest models.
A former racing driver founded it in northern Italy in the 1940s. Its factory is still in a small town near Modena.
It joined the New York Stock Exchange in October 2015, with a four-letter ticker symbol that describes what it does best: RACE.
A black horse standing on its back legs on a yellow background, and a lot of red.
The founder’s surname, a common Italian one that comes from the word for a blacksmith.

items.name: Nike
clues: It sells clothes and shoes for sport, but most of its customers have never run a marathon.
Runners, basketball fans, sneaker collectors who never take theirs out of the box, and people who wear tracksuits to the supermarket.
A young accountant and his old running coach started it in Oregon in 1964, and at first he sold Japanese running shoes from the boot of his car.
It joined the stock market in December 1980, and since 2013 it has been one of the 30 companies in the Dow Jones index.
A logo like a tick, which a design student drew for $35 in 1971.
It’s named after the Greek goddess of victory.

items.name: Netflix
clues: It sells you hours and hours of something for a fixed price every month, and then asks if you’re still there.
Students who say they’ll watch just one episode, couples who can’t agree what to watch, and anyone who has shared a password with an ex.
Two Americans started it in California in 1997, posting DVDs to people’s homes. In 2000 they offered to sell it to the biggest video-rental chain for $50 million, and were turned down.
It joined the Nasdaq in May 2002 at $15 a share. It started streaming in 2007, and its DVD-by-post service finally closed in 2023.
A red letter N on a black screen, and a deep “ta-dum” before every show.
“Net”, as in the internet, plus “flix”, slang for films.

items.name: Tesla
clues: It sells cars, but investors have often valued it more like a technology company than a carmaker.
People who want to show they care about the planet, and people who just like going very fast, very quietly.
Two engineers founded it in California in 2003. Its most famous boss joined the next year, as an investor.
It went public in June 2010 at $17 a share. In 2021 it became worth more than a trillion dollars.
A logo shaped like a T, and a factory in Grünheide, just outside Berlin, that opened in 2022.
It’s named after a Serbian-American inventor who worked on electricity.

items.name: Coca-Cola
clues: It sells something that is mostly water and sugar, in more than 200 countries.
Everyone, at least once. Especially at Christmas, if you believe the adverts.
A pharmacist created the drink in Atlanta in 1886.
The world’s most famous investor, Warren Buffett, started buying its shares in 1988 and has never sold them.
Red and white, with letters that look like old-fashioned handwriting, and a curvy glass bottle designed to be recognised even in the dark.
Its name comes from two of its original ingredients: coca leaves and kola nuts.

items.name: GameStop
clues: It sells video games and consoles in shops, which is now a slightly old-fashioned way to buy them.
Gamers, collectors and, in 2021, a huge crowd of small investors, many of whom had never bought a share before.
An American chain of shops, based near Dallas in Texas.
In January 2021 users of an online forum bought so many of its shares that the price rose more than tenfold in a few weeks, and hedge funds that had bet against it lost billions.
A man who called himself “Roaring Kitty” became the hero of the story, and in 2023 it was turned into the film Dumb Money.
Two words: what you play, and a place where you stop.
